rationale: Strong per-study batch effects (sequencing depth, 16S region, protocol) shift each genus's abundance distribution between studies, so one RF threshold doesn't carry across studies. This change converts each genus's relative abundance to a percentile rank within its own study. That only uses the data without labels, keeps the order of samples inside each study, and puts all studies on one shared scale before the forest is trained. I haven't run it here, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Lower gut-microbial diversity is one of the most consistent IBD findings across cohorts. A random forest on genus ranks has to rebuild that signal from hundreds of scattered genus splits, so I'm adding it directly. The new features are Shannon diversity at OTU and genus level, inverse Simpson, and depth-normalized richness (expected number of OTUs in a rarefied sample of 1000 reads), each converted to a percentile rank within its study like the genus features. Not run yet, so no Dev score.

The current genus parser keeps only the 6th lineage token. That merges every OTU with an empty genus (`g__`) into one column, whatever its family, so for example unclassified Lachnospiraceae and unclassified Enterobacteriaceae get added together. That wipes out signals known to matter in IBD, such as Enterobacteriaceae gain and Ruminococcaceae/Lachnospiraceae loss. I'm switching to taxonomy-aware aggregation: each feature is the full lineage prefix at phylum, class, order, family and genus level, so unclassified reads go to their deepest known parent. Identical duplicate columns are dropped, and the per-study rank harmonization stays as it was.

I'm adding one feature, Gevers' (2014) microbial dysbiosis index: the log-ratio of taxa that increase in IBD (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae, Neisseriaceae, Gemellaceae) to taxa that decrease (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales other than Veillonellaceae, Erysipelotrichaceae, Bifidobacteriaceae). It's ranked within each study like the other features. A random forest has to build this combined signal from many separate clade splits, so giving it the published index as one column should help, especially since Gevers' RISK cohort is one of the pooled studies. I haven't run it, so I don't have a Dev score yet.

I'm adding a prevalence filter that keeps a clade only if it is non-zero in at least 5% of samples in every study. Thousands of lineage-prefix clades are rare or only show up in some studies, because primers, 16S regions and depth differ. Within a study where a clade is absent, every sample gets the same rank of 0.5, so it carries no information there and is pure noise in the pooled data. With the forest's default of trying only sqrt(p) features per split, those noise columns crowd out the shared cross-study signal, so dropping them should help. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

Within each study and class (case or control), each training sample gets a weight inversely proportional to how many samples share its study and class, so every study counts equally and cases and controls count equally inside each study. Right now the largest study (Gevers RISK) and its case/control ratio dominate the forest's splits, but the score is within-study AUROC; balanced weights should push the forest toward signals that separate cases from controls in every study.

I'm adding an L2 logistic regression on the same per-study rank features and averaging its rank-normalized test predictions with the forest's. The main IBD signals (lower diversity, loss of Faecalibacterium/Roseburia/Ruminococcaceae, gain of Enterobacteriaceae) are mostly monotone and point the same way in every study. A linear model on harmonized ranks captures them directly and more stably than axis-aligned forest splits, and its errors should be fairly uncorrelated with the forest's. The regularization strength is picked by inner grouped CV on the training fold, using the same study × class balanced weights. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

IBD dysbiosis shows up as a sample moving away from the healthy community (the "Anna Karenina" pattern seen in Gevers and Halfvarson), not only as shifts in single taxa. So I'm adding one label-aware feature computed inside each training fold: the mean distance from each sample to its 10 nearest training controls in the same study, measured on the per-study rank features. Training samples skip themselves and other samples from the same subject, so their distances are measured the same way as for test samples. The distance is then turned into a within-study percentile and fed to both the forest and the logistic regression. Not run yet, so there is no Dev score.

I'm adding a third model to the rank-averaged ensemble: a shallow, heavily regularized LightGBM gradient-boosted tree model on the same per-study rank features, using the same study × class balanced weights. In this dysbiosis signal, effects depend on each other (for example, Enterobacteriaceae gain matters most when Faecalibacterium/Roseburia are depleted and diversity is low). Boosting fits these joint patterns step by step, correcting what earlier trees missed, while the forest averages independent trees and logistic regression is purely additive. Its errors should therefore overlap only partly with the other two, which should help the average. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it.

I'm replacing the random forest with ExtraTrees (1000 trees). Everything else stays the same: features, per-study ranks, study × class weights, the inner-CV-tuned L2 logistic regression and the rank-averaging. On per-study rank features, the IBD signal is spread across many correlated clades (the butyrate-producing Clostridiales and their parent clades, plus the diversity measures). The forest's split thresholds, each chosen to fit the training fold best, overfit to study-specific quirks. ExtraTrees picks thresholds at random and trains on the full sample, which spreads importance over correlated clades and gives smoother, more monotone scores that should hold up better within each study and add more to the linear model.

ExtraTrees currently considers only sqrt(p) of the roughly 300 rank features at each split. Because ExtraTrees already varies its trees through random cut-points, I'm raising `max_features` to 0.3. More candidate features per split should help the trees pick the weak but consistent clades and diversity measures that separate IBD cases in every study. That should also make the forest scores more within-study discriminative and less noisy before they are rank-averaged with the logistic regression. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

Only the logistic regression's input changes. Its per-study percentile ranks are converted to normal scores (inverse-normal, clipped to 0.01–0.99) instead of being centered uniformly at 0.5. The IBD signal is concentrated in the tails of each study's distribution, such as Enterobacteriaceae blooms and near-total loss of Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and diversity. Uniform ranks squeeze those extremes together, while normal scores give them more weight in the additive model. ExtraTrees is left unchanged, since it is invariant to monotone transforms. The C grid is widened downward because the new features have a larger scale, and C is still chosen by inner grouped CV. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

The score is AUROC within each study, but each model's predictions are currently ranked across the whole pooled test fold. If one model's scores shift between studies, global ranking spends that model's resolution on the gaps between studies instead of on separating samples inside a study. This change ranks each model's test predictions within their own study (using test-set study labels only, no outcome labels) before averaging, so both models count equally inside every study, which is where the score is measured.

Add species-level lineage clades to the taxonomy hierarchy. Known IBD signals sit at species level, inside genera that otherwise mix them with unrelated species: Ruminococcus gnavus goes up while other Lachnospiraceae Ruminococcus do not, Faecalibacterium prausnitzii goes down, and Escherichia coli and Bacteroides fragilis also matter. Species that are the only named member of their genus are removed by the existing duplicate-column filter, and rare ones by the cross-study prevalence filter, so only species-level splits that are measurable in every study are added. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score yet.

In round 11, raising ExtraTrees `max_features` from sqrt(p) to 0.3 cut the Dev score by 0.011. That suggests the forest gains from more decorrelated trees, not from greedier splits. So this round goes the other way: `max_features="log2"` (about 8 of the ~300 per-study rank features per split, down from about 17). That makes the weak but consistent clades and diversity measures share more of the forest's vote, which should give smoother scores within each study. I also raised `n_estimators` to 1500 to absorb the extra per-tree variance. This hasn't been run, so there is no Dev score yet.

Right now each study's features are ranked against all of that study's samples. That reference depends on each study's case/control ratio, so the same rank means something different in each study. I'm switching to control-referenced percentile normalization (Gibbons, Duvallet & Alm 2018, designed for microbiome case-control meta-analysis). Inside `fit_predict`, each sample's features are re-expressed as percentiles of its study's training-fold controls. Every study's healthy distribution then sits on the same scale, and dysbiosis becomes a departure from local controls that is comparable across studies for both models. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

`groups_train` shows that some subjects contribute several samples, so a few heavily sampled patients (mostly from the longitudinal cohorts) carry most of their stratum's training weight and both models learn their individual microbiomes. The change makes each subject count equally inside its study × class stratum (each sample gets 1/samples-of-its-subject, renormalized so every stratum keeps its current total weight). The models should then learn disease signals shared across patients, which is what transfers to the new subjects in the grouped test folds. If no subject has repeat samples, the weights come out exactly as before. I haven't run this, so I don't have a Dev score for it yet.

Within a study, read depth varies a lot between samples. A deep sample picks up low-abundance clades that a shallow sample from the same study reports as zero, so the bottom of each per-study rank mostly reflects depth rather than biology. Before ranking and prevalence filtering, I'll apply one detection limit per study: a clade is counted only if its relative abundance is at least 1/D_s, where D_s is the 10th-percentile read depth of that study. This only uses the data without labels and keeps presence/absence of a clade, such as loss of Faecalibacterium or Roseburia, comparable across samples in the same study. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.

I'm adding one feature block: centered log-ratio (CLR) values for genera, with pseudocount 0.5. It uses only genera that pass the cross-study prevalence filter, and each value is ranked within its study like the existing features. Relative abundance is a closed composition, so an Enterobacteriaceae or Proteobacteria bloom pushes down every other clade's share and rank, which mixes "a bloom happened" with "butyrate producers were lost". CLR measures each genus against the sample's geometric mean, so one bloom barely moves the other genera. That gives both models a second view of loss of Faecalibacterium, Roseburia and Ruminococcaceae, separate from the bloom signal. I haven't run this, so there is no Dev score for it yet.

ExtraTrees currently grows every tree until each leaf is pure, so single samples define leaves. Those include atypical or mislabeled ones (e.g. IBD in remission) and heavily weighted samples from the small studies, so the forest's scores pick up per-sample noise. Requiring at least 3 samples per leaf (`min_samples_leaf=3`) averages each leaf over a few similar samples. That should give smoother, more monotone dysbiosis scores that rank better within each study and blend better with the logistic regression. It only changes how deep the trees grow; earlier rounds changed the features tried per split (`max_features`), which seems to be at its best value already. I haven't run it, so there is no Dev score yet.
